item.title: Flow and transport characteristics of hydrogen in a square-spiral Knudsen pump with coupled thermal transpiration and Poiseuille flow
item.description: arXiv:2611.04288v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gas transport driven by thermal transpiration under temperature gradients, known as a Knudsen pump, has shown strong potential in gas separation and delivery applications. However, its performance and operational stability are strongly affected by structural design, system integration, and manufacturing complexity, highlighting the need for efficient and manufacturable multi-stage configurations. In this study, a novel spiral-structured Knudsen pump is proposed. Within the microchannels, a temperature gradient drives gas from the low- to high-temperature region, inducing pressure rise and thermal transpiration. In the main channel, a pressure gradient drives gas from the high- to low-temperature region, forming Poiseuille flow. Numerical methods are employed to investigate the flow mechanisms, and the effects of varying the numbers of series and parallel microchannels on gas transmission behavior are evaluated. The results indicate that bends of the main channel lead to nonlinear variations in pressure and temperature, as well as flow deceleration in the curved regions. Increasing the number of serial channels reduces the pressure load across the microchannel, thereby enhancing the overall transport performance. For instance, a ten-stage serial configuration improves performance by 3.35% compared with the four-stage case, reaching 3.10E10-7 kg/(m*s). In contrast, increasing the number of parallel microchannels reduces pressure loading while enhancing gas rarefaction, thereby strengthening thermal transpiration. A five-stage parallel configuration yields an 70.80% improvement over the two-stage case, reaching 3.07E10-7 kg/(m*s). These results provide valuable guidance for the design and fabrication of high-performance Knudsen pumps.
item.dc:creator: Yawei Huang, Jianjun Ye, Junlong Xie, Jian Xiao, Dinggen Li, Xuesong He

item.title: Transitional Fluid-Ablation Interactions on a Compression Ramp at Mach 8
item.description: arXiv:2611.04443v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Direct numerical simulations (DNS) are performed for a Mach 8 flow over a 15 degree compression ramp undergoing ablation to analyze fluid-ablation interaction (FAI) effects on instability growth and transition of the high-speed boundary layer. Wind-tunnel experiments at these conditions show characteristic heating streaks which are first replicated for laminar flow over an inert ramp. Perturbations superimposed on the laminar baseflow are informed by stability calculations. The ramp is then replaced by a low-temperature ablator in our DNS and the interaction of the streaks with the ablating surface is examined. Ablation models implemented in two independently-developed fluid dynamics solvers are used to study this problem. Overall, both solvers have shown an excellent agreement regarding heat fluxes, mass blowing rates, and recession patterns. Numerical experiments are performed to assess the impact of accelerating recession and of higher amplitude perturbations. We demonstrate accurate predictions of ablative recession and present novel findings regarding its influence on the perturbation evolution for this configuration.
item.dc:creator: Ata Onur Ba\c{s}kaya, Sean Dungan, Stefan Hickel, Christoph Brehm

item.title: Fluid memory beyond creeping flow: a history kernel for a sphere at finite Reynolds numbers
item.description: arXiv:2611.04606v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Predicting the history force on a sphere beyond the creeping-flow limit remains challenging. Existing formulations have been derived or calibrated for selected flow histories, with limited evidence of their predictive accuracy under more general conditions. We develop a systematic approach to extract the history kernel of a fixed sphere in spatially uniform, unsteady flow from axisymmetric Navier-Stokes simulations of finite-duration acceleration and deceleration ramps at initial Reynolds numbers from 0.2 to 200. The resulting kernel surface recovers the Basset limit at short lags and in the creeping-flow limit and is continued beyond the resolved lags using far-wake asymptotics. At higher Reynolds numbers, the kernel develops non-monotonic behaviour at intermediate lags, associated with delayed adjustment of the boundary layer and wake. For the cases tested, the present kernel substantially improves history-force predictions for finite ramps, oscillatory forcing and non-periodic composite velocity histories relative to the literature formulations considered, without case-specific adjustment. These findings indicate that lag and Reynolds number capture the dominant memory response.
item.dc:creator: M. D. {\L}asica, J. G. M. Kuerten, S. K. F. Stoter

item.title: A flux-balanced diffuse-interface kinetic model for rarefied gas-solid boundaries with arbitrary absorption probability
item.description: arXiv:2611.04622v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rarefied gas--solid interactions determine mechanical loads, heat transfer, and material exchange in microscale devices and low-pressure processings. Modeling these interactions becomes challenging when gas non-equilibrium effect and complex moving boundaries must be resolved together. We develop a diffuse-interface kinetic model (DIKM) that describes rarefied gas transport and gas--solid interactions in one kinetic formulation on a single fixed Eulerian mesh. A smooth order parameter represents solid geometry, while a localized molecular flux operator incorporates boundary interactions directly into the kinetic equation by distinguishing incident and reflected distributions in the interface region and specifying their mass, momentum, and energy exchange, including prescribed surface absorption. Matched asymptotic analysis shows that the diffuse formulation recovers the corresponding partially absorbing diffuse-reflection boundary condition for smooth stationary or moving surfaces in the sharp-interface limit. Discretization uses Strang splitting, combining an order-parameter-weighted discrete unified gas kinetic scheme for the transport substep with a positivity-preserving update of the interfacial source. Benchmarks over planar and curved, stationary and moving boundaries reproduce rarefaction-dependent velocity slip and wall heat transfer, absorption-driven flow, and feedback between gas forces and solid translation and rotation. In final simulations, the order parameter evolves by a Cahn--Hilliard equation with degenerate mobility, and thin-film growth exhibits distinct surface profiles at different vapor incidence angles. By connecting implicit geometry to molecular surface exchange, DIKM provides a basis for coupling rarefied gas dynamics to solid motion and material evolution.
item.dc:creator: Chujin Qin, Dongke Sun

item.title: On flow unsteadiness in strongly separated high-speed ramp flows using kinetic and data-driven methods
item.description: arXiv:2611.04684v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The gas dynamics of high speed flows over several compression-expansion ramp geometries with large separation regions were investigated using a particle kinetic approach and data driven methods. These large separation regions allow study of the role of scaled angle predicted by triple deck theory on recirculation strength, separation size, and appearance of secondary recirculation regions, all of which lead to flow unsteadiness. Examining four different free stream conditions for the same geometry using the direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) approach, we show that the stability of single recirculation in the separation region is more sensitive to wall temperature and free stream velocity than physical ramp angle. Stability in this context refers to appearance of secondary separation regions. In addition, configurations with similar types of recirculation regions from literature considered, we find that general trends regarding unsteadiness, such as appearance of secondary recirculation regions, mostly hold; however, the flows are too complex to be characterized by only scaled angle. Thus, stochastic flowfields generated by DSMC were investigated using data driven methods, namely spectral proper orthogonal decomposition and dynamic mode decomposition. We found that both methods yield similar frequency components and mode shapes for spatio-temporal coherent structures of unsteady DSMC flows. With the help of these structures, the main mechanisms of unsteadiness were identified as oscillations of the reattachment shock, Kelvin-Helmholtz like instability of the shear layer, and c-shaped mode of the separation bubble. This is the first time SPOD has been applied to a DSMC generated flowfield and compared with DMD.
item.dc:creator: Irmak Taylan Karpuzcu, Mert Senkardesler, Deborah A. Levin

item.title: Designing turbulence through hierarchies
item.description: arXiv:2611.04706v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Turbulence is defined by a set of emergent and singular phenomena: a constant-flux energy cascade, intermittency, a dissipation rate that survives the vanishing of viscosity, and the spontaneous loss of determinism of the inviscid limit. Which physical ingredients produce them remains unclear, because in fluids they always come together with incompressibility, spatial structure and vortex dynamics. Here we show that a hierarchy of inertia, coupled by the purely geometric nonlinearity of rigid constraints, is enough. A planar chain of rigid pendula whose lengths and masses decrease geometrically, coupled only through nearest-neighbor constraints, develops a far-from-equilibrium cascade that replaces thermal equipartition, with statistically local and time-irreversible energy transfer despite intrinsically nonlocal coupling. Its fluctuations are intermittent, yet self-similarity is restored by a hidden scale symmetry. As the viscosity vanishes, the dissipation rate saturates at a finite value, and thermal noise consistent with fluctuation-dissipation balance is amplified from the smallest to the largest scales within a fraction of a large-scale period. Because the hierarchy can be tuned and the same dynamics can be realized mechanically or electrically, turbulence becomes a property that can be designed and measured in the laboratory.
item.dc:creator: Flavio Tuteri, Andr\'e Freitas

item.title: Reconstructing Rayleigh--B\'enard flows from temperature-only measurements using the Ensemble Kalman Filter
item.description: arXiv:2611.04795v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reconstructing the full state of a multiscale chaotic system from observations of only a subset of its degrees of freedom is a central problem in data assimilation. Turbulent Rayleigh--B\'enard convection offers a paradigmatic example, for which Charney conjectured that temperature measurements alone should suffice to determine the velocity field. Synchronization-based methods such as nudging and direct replacement nonetheless fail in chaotic regimes, because they require the measurement of the determining modes of the system, a set to which the velocity belongs but the temperature does not. Here we show that the Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF), equipped with a proper inflation scheme, removes this asymmetry by exploiting the flow-dependent cross-covariances between temperature and vorticity, and recovers the velocity from noisy and spatio-temporally sparse temperature data alone. We assess the filter in two chaotic regimes of two-dimensional bulk convection by means of a scale-by-scale spectral analysis. When the whole temperature field is observed, both fields synchronize with the true state at all resolved scales, with the temperature estimate becoming even more accurate than the measurements themselves for sufficiently frequent observations. Equispaced observation networks preserve this full-spectrum synchronization down to a threshold density, below which only the largest scales remain synchronized, as also happens when observations are confined to a subdomain. We conclude that Charney's conjecture is numerically verified in two-dimensional turbulent convection when the assimilation is performed using a properly calibrated EnKF.
item.dc:creator: Francesco Fossella, Luca Biferale, Alberto Carrassi, Massimo Cencini, Mathieu Desbrun, Kiwon Um

item.title: The Nonlinear Physics and Statistical Field Theory of Twilight Clouds: Hovering Dynamics and Dynamic Inertia Emergence
item.description: arXiv:2611.04924v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Twilight clouds are small, optically faint warm clouds whose droplets fluctuate between haze and activated growth. We develop a nonequilibrium statistical field theory linking this regime to cloud-field organization through K\"ohler microphysics, supersaturation transport, and turbulent mixing. At parcel level, supersaturation rapidly tracks slow droplet growth with a finite lag. Mixing-induced supersaturation removal drives a saddle-node bifurcation, shifting the activation threshold and supporting intermittent hovering under turbulent fluctuations. Starting from turbulent transport of supersaturation coupled to droplet growth, we derive a droplet-supersaturation field system and formulate it within the Martin-Siggia-Rose framework. A Gurari-type variational reduction inspired by polaron theory eliminates the fast bath. Turbulence dresses the slow droplet field, shrinks the forbidden zone below the equilibrium curve, and raises the mixing threshold required to suppress activation. Each droplet population induces a screened supersaturation halo that couples neighboring cloud elements; its delayed adjustment generates dynamic inertia and temporally correlated noise. The resulting nonlinear, non-Markovian pseudoparabolic stochastic equation has a bounded frozen-background response at short wavelengths. Its long-wave coupling amplifies contrasts where the dressed slow manifold turns downward. Comparisons with the parent two-field system show that a spatially correlated Markovian closure preserves droplet-radius distributions and cloudlet organization. Near the activation fold, restoring residual-bath fluctuation memory improves recurrent-hovering frequency and patch extent without recalibrating the drift or fitting a correlation time. More broadly, the framework identifies how slow fields acquire interactions and inertia through the relaxing, diffusive environments they modify.
item.dc:creator: Micka\"el D. Chekroun, Ilan Koren

item.title: Lagrangian Irreversibility in Stratified Turbulence
item.description: arXiv:2611.05282v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stable stratification reorganizes turbulence, suppressing vertical motion and altering the balance between vortical and strain-dominated flow structures. How these changes affect the temporal asymmetry of kinetic-energy exchange along fluid-particle trajectories remains incompletely understood. Using direct numerical simulations of homogeneous Boussinesq turbulence, we investigate Lagrangian power statistics across four local velocity-gradient topology classes and three nonzero stratification strengths, with an unstratified reference case. With increasing stratification, the global power variance decreases while the standardized skewness becomes more negative, indicating enhanced asymmetry despite weaker fluctuations. Conditioning on local topology reveals distinct responses: axial-strain-dominated regions exhibit the most negative total-power skewness at all stratification strengths, whereas biaxial-strain-dominated regions change sign from positive to negative under stratification. Horizontal and vertical component powers also respond differently, revealing directional dependence. Among the dynamical contributions to power, the pressure contribution, nearly symmetric in the unstratified case, becomes more negatively skewed with increasing stratification. Energy-conditioned pressure statistics further indicate altered pressure-mediated energy redistribution. Finally, tracer persistence-time distributions exhibit exponential tails, with time scales that differ across topology classes and respond differently to stratification. Increasing stratification is thus accompanied by three concurrent changes: enhanced asymmetry of Lagrangian power, modified energy redistribution by pressure, and altered temporal sampling of local flow structures by tracers. These co-occurring signatures characterize the response to stratification, though their causal relations remain to be established.
item.dc:creator: Mrinal Jyoti Powdel, Samriddhi Sankar Ray

item.title: Shock wave transmission across solid-water interfaces in underwater electrical foil explosions
item.description: arXiv:2611.03657v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The transmission of shock waves generated by underwater electrical foil explosions across solid materials with varying acoustic impedances and thicknesses is investigated. Copper foils with thicknesses of 10 and 18 $\mu$m are exploded on planar substrates of aluminum, copper, and 3D-printed PLA with thicknesses up to 5 mm using a multi-gigawatt pulsed-power electrical discharge. The resulting shocks are visualized in water using high-speed shadowgraphy at 5 million frames per second, while high-resolution fiber optic hydrophone measurements provide direct quantitative measurements of shock strength after transmission through the impedance-mismatched materials. One-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations are used to reproduce the foil explosion dynamics and provide insight into the thermodynamic, acoustic, and electrical properties of the foil during the explosion. The results show that shock transmission is governed not only by the impedance mismatch at the solid--water interface but also by the finite thickness and dynamic response of the supporting material. These findings provide a quantitative framework for understanding and controlling shock transmission in underwater electrical foil explosions and establish the feasibility and limitations of using solid substrates as structural supports in complex shock-generating geometries.
item.dc:creator: Francesc Hern\'andez Garcia, Brian Bertacco, Tobia De Benedictis, Sebasti\'an Rojas Mata, Jergus Strucka, Michael Liverts

item.title: Physics-Informed Identification of Tensegrity Prestress across Taut-Slack Transitions
item.description: arXiv:2611.04007v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Prestress governs the stability, stiffness, and dynamic behavior of tensegrity structures, but it is not directly observable from sparse structural measurements, and it may decrease during service life. Under strong excitation, the cables may slacken and the dynamics become nonsmooth. Existing identification methods are limited to the taut regime, and physics-informed networks for tensegrities solve only the forward problem of predicting the response from known member parameters. This study formulates the inverse problem. Neural networks are trained on the equation-of-motion residual in constrained Cartesian coordinates, where the mass matrix is constant and the force densities enter linearly. The force densities, damping, and axial stiffness are trainable parameters, and the tension-only cable law is kept. A Fisher-information analysis shows, before inversion, which member parameters a record can determine. The method is tested on simulated planar tensegrity frames with up to five modules and a three-dimensional prism, and on measured records of a biomimetic leg and a full-scale tensegrity simplex. On the one-module frame, the identifiable force densities are recovered within 1.5% from noisy accelerations at half the free coordinates, on records with and without taut-slack transitions. Records with transitions determine members that taut records leave undetermined. On the five-module frame, a 16-cable two-span bridge, the median force-density error rises moderately, to 4.2%. On measured records, an identified spring stiffness is within 0.1% of its independently measured value on average, and the identified simplex prestress at 13 levels agrees with its cable force transducers to 2.9% root-mean-square.
item.dc:creator: Sandesh Lamsal, Sumit Kumar, Rubi Bhandari, Subhamoy Sen, Andrzej Rutkiewicz, Leszek Ma{\l}yszko, Landolf Rhode-Barbarigos

item.title: From Sea Surface Height to Velocity - A Machine Learning Approach
item.description: arXiv:2611.04270v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Inferring upper-ocean velocity from altimetric sea surface height (SSH) remains challenging below 50~km, scales now resolved by the Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) mission. Conventional methods rely on geostrophic or cyclogeostrophic balance. Here, we demonstrate that deep learning can predict the full velocity vector from SSH and environmental data and recover derivative-based diagnostics, including spectral energy flux. We trained a U-Net encoder--decoder on hourly fields from the pre-SWOT Cape Basin extraction of the LLC4320 ocean simulation, with 1.5-km grid spacing ($11.8$--$15.8^\circ$E, $41$--$45^\circ$S). Inputs were SSH, sea surface temperature (SST), and wind stress; targets were horizontal velocities at the surface and 50~m, where wind influence is weaker. At 50~m, the best model achieves a speed RMSE of $0.049\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, 29% lower than the geostrophic approximation. Predicted relative vorticity has a correlation of 0.93, compared with 0.75 for the geostrophic approximation. The model also recovers divergence with a correlation of 0.66, whereas geostrophic velocity is nondivergent by definition. Tests of training strategies yield four findings: SSH gradients outperform raw SSH as inputs; wind stress is the most useful covariate for total velocity prediction; SST benefits vary seasonally; and including vorticity and divergence in the loss improves accuracy. These results offer a path for transferring high-fidelity simulation physics to SWOT applications, where kilometer-scale SSH snapshots contain superposed balanced and unbalanced signals.
item.dc:creator: Yaswanth Reddy Yaradoddi, Jinbo Wang, Elyes Serghine

item.title: High-order compact ALE gas-kinetic scheme on three-dimensional unstructured meshes
item.description: arXiv:2611.05095v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper, a compact high-order gas-kinetic scheme (HGKS) is developed for compressible arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian (ALE) computations on three-dimensional unstructured meshes. To achieve high-order spatial accuracy, a large number of matrix inversions are required for spatial reconstruction. In ALE computations, the mesh moves and the geometric information must be recalculated at each time step, which reduces computational efficiency. To improve efficiency, a memory-reduction reconstruction strategy is employed to construct a quadratic polynomial on unstructured meshes. By differentiating the candidate polynomial, the quadratic terms are obtained by the least-squares method using the average gradient values of the cell itself and its neighboring cells. The linear terms of the polynomial are also determined by the least-squares method. On three-dimensional unstructured meshes, a $3\times3$ coefficient matrix must be stored, and four least-squares procedures are required to construct a quadratic polynomial. To suppress numerical oscillations in flows with discontinuities, generalized essentially non-oscillatory (GENO) reconstruction and a gradient compression factor are adopted. To accelerate the computation, a multi-GPU accelerated code is implemented using Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA) and Message Passing Interface (MPI). The current scheme is fully explicit, and the acceleration framework can be developed based on cell-level parallelism. Numerical examples are presented to evaluate the accuracy and robustness of the scheme, including flows with strong discontinuities, pitching wings, and helicopter rotors. Numerical results confirm the excellent performance of the compact ALE scheme on unstructured meshes.
item.dc:creator: Yibo Wang, Xing Ji, Liang Pan

item.title: Statistical State Dynamics based study of turbulence in Eady fronts. Part 1. Instability
item.description: arXiv:2506.11993v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The streamwise roll and streak structure (RSS) is prominent in observations of the planetary boundary layer in the atmosphere and ocean and in unstratified wall-bounded shear flows. Although the RSS in these systems is structurally similar, the mechanism forming and maintaining the RSS in both remains controversial. This study demonstrates that the same turbulence-sustaining mechanism identified to underlie the RSS in the Statistical State Dynamics (SSD) formulation of unstratified wall-bounded shear flow dynamics (Farrell & Ioannou 2012; Farrell et al. 2016) also operates in the Eady front. We analyze the mechanism by which turbulence and symmetric instability interact to form the RSS in the baroclinic stratified Eady front model by adapting to the Eady front problem the stability analysis of the second order closure of the SSD used previously to study roll formation in unstratified wall-bounded shear flows. Our findings advance mechanistic understanding of RSS formation in the turbulent geostrophic front regime and establish foundational parallels between geophysical turbulent front dynamics and turbulence dynamics in engineering-scale shear flows.
item.dc:creator: Eojin Kim, Brian F. Farrell

item.title: Statistical state dynamics based study of turbulent Eady fronts. Part 2. Finite amplitude equilibria
item.description: arXiv:2507.15134v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Streamwise roll circulations commonly observed in frontal regions are primary agents of momentum and tracer transport in the planetary boundary layer (PBL) both in the atmosphere and ocean. Traditionally, the formation of the streamwise roll/streak structure (RSS) has been ascribed to symmetric instability (SI). In part 1, we studied RSS formation in the classical Eady front problem using statistical state dynamics (SSD), which allows incorporating the Reynolds stress (RS) torque instability mechanism together with SI in the dynamics underlying RSS formation. We found using SSD theory that the RS torque mechanism acts synergistically with the SI mechanism in forcing symmetric circulations in fronts when Richardson number Ri < 1, and also that the turbulence-mediated RS torque mechanism supports RSS formation in fronts with Ri > 1 for which the SI mechanism does not operate. Although SI theory provides an explanation for initial roll formation, it leaves open the question of RSS equilibration. An advantage of the SSD formulation of RSS dynamics is that it consistently incorporates the equilibration process. In this paper, we extend perturbation analysis of RSS dynamics in the SSD framework to a nonlinear analysis to understand roll formation, equilibration, and maintenance in the turbulent RSS regime.
item.dc:creator: Eojin Kim, Brian F. Farrell

item.title: Multi-Partitioned Computing Quantum-Particle Approach: A Hybrid Quantum Framework for Fluid Flow
item.description: arXiv:2509.11276v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This study established a quantum-classical hybrid framework that integrates quantum computing paradigm with meshfree finite particle method. By harnessing quantum superposition and entanglement, it hybridized the critical computational kernels (termed as quantum finite particle method). A resource-efficient quantum computational strategy on multi-partitioned zones was proposed, which leverages a fixed small-scale quantum circuit as a fundamental processing unit to handle inner product for arbitrarily sized arrays. This approach employs iterative nesting of the quantum-core operation to accommodate varying input dimensions while maintaining hardware feasibility throughout. Motivated with developed quantum framework, the novel numerical discretization for hybrid quantum computational particle dynamics can be derived commonly and applied in fluid flows. Through a sequence of numerical experiments purposefully, the proposed numerical model was thoroughly validated and analyzed. Results demonstrate that integrating quantum computing to hybridize conventional linear combinations of particle dynamics serves as a novel computing paradigm. By further extending into the numerical investigation of viscoelastic, highly elastic, and purely elastic fluids under high Weissenberg number conditions, the applicability of simulation framework is broadened. Despite bottlenecks in quantum hardware and computational efficiency on this process, these advances offer critical insights for transitioning quantum-enhanced fluid simulation to practical engineering applications.
item.dc:creator: Yudong Li, Wenkui Shi, Zhihao Qian, Yan Li, Chunfa Wang, Ling Tao, Zhuojia Fu, Moubin Liu, Zhiqiang Feng

item.title: Small-Scale Dynamo for Full Spectrum of Hydrodynamic Turbulence in Kazantsev Model
item.description: arXiv:2604.01718v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A method is proposed for computing coefficients in the Kazantsev equation of small-scale dynamo for the full spectrum of hydromagnetic turbulence comprising the inertial range together with the range of viscous dissipation. The dynamo equation with so-defined coefficients is solved numerically for magnetic (Rm) and hydrodynamic (Re) Reynolds numbers from $10^2$ to $10^8$. The threshold value ${\rm Rm}_c$ for onset of dynamo increases initially with Re but then saturates at a constant value of ${\rm Rm}_c \simeq 300$ for ${\rm Re}\geq 10^5$. In the case of small Prandtl number Pm = Rm/Re << 1, the field growth rate is also small and depends logarithmically on Rm. In this case, the magnetic energy spectrum peaks around the scale of Ohmic dissipation, which decreases with increasing Pm. The decrease stops at the scale of viscous dissipation while the growth rate increases sharply when Pm approaches the value of one. The increase in the growth rate proceeds to ${\rm Pm} > 1$ but slows down and then saturates at a value somewhat below the inverse lifetime of most short-living eddies. An explanation of the results is proposed.
item.dc:creator: Leonid Kitchatinov

item.title: Interaction of vortex rings generated by two unsynchronised drop impacts
item.description: arXiv:2607.07214v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A liquid drop falling into a pool can create a vortex ring at the right impact conditions. Such drop-formed vortex rings are of importance in nature and technology and the dynamics of rings created by single and synchronised double drop impacts have been extensively studied. In practice, two neighbouring drops rarely impact a liquid surface exactly at the same time, yet the interaction of two unsynchronised vortex rings have not been studied. Here, we have performed experiments with two water drops impacting a water pool at varying time differences $\Delta t$. By using particle image velocimetry, we have quantified the time-evolution of the resulting vortex rings. We find four distinct categories of vortex ring evolution depending on $\Delta t$. At $\Delta t<0.5$ ms, fully symmetric merging of the vortex rings occur. At unsynchronisation larger than this, the merging either becomes asymmetric and incomplete ($0.5 < \Delta t<7$ ms) or non-existent ($\Delta t \geq 7$ ms). At $7 \leq \Delta t<80$ ms, the creation of the second vortex ring is impaired, whereas at $\Delta t\geq 80$ ms, the first impact no longer affects the formation of the second ring and the two rings evolve without influencing each other. We show that these regimes can be explained by the capillary waves created by the first droplet. Our results demonstrate the importance of the time difference between drop impacts in the creation and subsequent interaction of two adjacent drop-formed vortex rings, which is important for achieving uniform and controlled mixing in high-throughput applications.
item.dc:creator: Anna A. L. Huttunen, Guilherme Moreira Bessa, Matilda Backholm

item.title: When can buoyancy be neglected in simulations of crystallization fouling? Evidence from a confluence flow cell
item.description: arXiv:2610.07305v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Predicting crystallization fouling remains difficult because it couples supersaturation, nucleation, crystal growth, transport, and adhesion. Separating these processes requires model systems in which they can be independently controlled. One such system is the confluence flow cell, where two incompatible brines mix and generate supersaturation at their interface. The mixing pattern is often predicted using constant-density simulations because density differences between the brines are typically only a few percent or less. We investigate whether this assumption holds when calcium chloride and sodium sulfate react to form gypsum. A constant-density simulation predicts deposition on the channel floor along the centreline. Experimentally, however, gypsum forms bands on both side walls, with deposition moving upstream as flow rate decreases. Dye experiments spanning density differences of 0.14 to 2.1 %, three channel heights, and 32 flow rates show that the distance required for the dyed stream to reach the opposite wall is governed by the bulk Richardson number, $Ri=g'H/U^2$, following $L/H = 3.31\,Ri^{-0.66}$ over four decades in Ri ($R^2=0.89$). When the stream densities are matched, the dyed stream typically no longer reaches the opposite wall, and a reacting experiment shows gypsum deposition on the floor, consistent with the constant-density simulation. A small density difference alone is therefore insufficient to neglect buoyancy; the Richardson number must also be small. At the low flow rates typical of confluence flow cells, this condition is often not met. Because Ri depends only on density difference, channel height, and flow velocity, we recommend evaluating it before applying constant-density models of mixing, reaction, or fouling.
item.dc:creator: Isaac Appelquist L{\o}ge, Candela Almaz\'an P\'erez, Maike W. Baltussen, Nadia Shardt

item.title: Emergent odd response in active chiral films
item.description: arXiv:2607.17717v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Active chiral fluids can support an anomalous transport coefficient known as odd (or Hall) viscosity. Hydrodynamic descriptions of such fluids typically introduce odd viscosity phenomenologically. How such a response emerges from specific microscopic interactions remains incompletely understood. Here, building on classical shear rheology, we microscopically derive an odd rheological response in active chiral films: thin layers of torque-exerting, elongated particles anchored to a no-slip surface. A canonical realization of such a film is the bacterial carpet, in which flagellated bacteria are tethered head-down to a solid surface while their flagella remain free to spin and inject angular momentum into the surrounding fluid. Using a Smoluchowski kinetic theory for the orientational dynamics of these anchored particles, we derive their stress response to an imposed shear flow. We reveal that shear-induced reorientation leads to a flow-aligned polarization and a transverse surface traction from which the odd-viscosity tensor follows in closed form. This approach stands in contrast with existing microscopic theories, in which the axis of torque injection is insensitive to the flow rather than set by it. Numerical solutions of the kinetic theory further highlight saturation of the transverse traction at strong shear, driven by this orientation dynamics -- signaling departure from linear response. Our results demonstrate how odd viscosity can emerge self-consistently as a coarse-grained rheological signature of active fluid-structure interaction and establish active chiral films as a new controllable setting for odd hydrodynamics.
item.dc:creator: Seema Chahal, Naveen Kumar D, Brato Chakrabarti
